questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Traditional Notions of Security' refers to.
questions.a: Traditional security centres the state and external military threats: greatest danger is war and violence from other states, and responses run through balance of power and alliance building, with deterrence and defense as the chief policy instruments including nuclear deterrence.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Traditional Notions of Security'.
questions.a: Security here means protecting the state - sovereignty, territory and population - from foreign military force.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Traditional Notions of Security' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Traditional Notions: External (source: leps105.txt traditional security, balance of power and deterrence sections)

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Non-traditional Notions of Security' refers to.
questions.a: Non-traditional security widens the referent to people and humanity: human security covers terrorism, human rights, global poverty and epidemics; global security addresses climate change, international terrorism and health epidemics that cross borders and threaten individuals more than armies do.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Non-traditional Notions of Security'.
questions.a: When threats come from germs, warming or terror networks, armies are the wrong instrument and people, not just states, are the protected.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Non-traditional Notions of Security' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Non-traditional Notions (source: leps105.txt human security, global poverty, epidemics and climate sections)

concepts.title: New Sources: Terrorism and Human Rights

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'New Sources: Terrorism and Human Rights' refers to.
questions.a: New threats include international terrorism by non-state networks, human rights abuses within states that the world may judge, and migration pressures; debates ask when the international community may act inside a sovereign state for humanitarian protection.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'New Sources: Terrorism and Human Rights'.
questions.a: Terror networks and rights abuses challenge both sovereignty's shield and the state's monopoly over security talk.

questions.q: Under which section is 'New Sources: Terrorism and Human Rights' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: New Sources of Threats (source: leps105.txt terrorism, human rights and migration threat sections)

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Cooperative Security and India's Strategy' refers to.
questions.a: Non-traditional threats demand cooperative security - joint action through institutions and agreements rather than force; India's security strategy combines strengthening military capabilities, internal security against separatism and terrorism, and developing the economy so that no citizen feels excluded.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Cooperative Security and India's Strategy'.
questions.a: India's three-pillar strategy - strength, internal stability and development - shows security as capability plus inclusion.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Cooperative Security and India's Strategy' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Cooperative Security (source: leps105.txt cooperative security and India's three-pillar strategy sections)
